visuals.label: Figure 1
visuals.caption: DreamX learns a shared action interface from egocentric human videos and robot videos. Compact, embodiment-agnostic latent actions extracted from a pretrained video diffusion model capture motion consistently across changes in embodiment and scene appearance. The same representation enables transferring motion from a source video to a target video, decoding hu- man motion into executable robot actions without paired human–robot training data, and training a lightweight latent policy that jointly predicts latent actions and robot actions.

visuals.label: Figure 2
visuals.caption: DreamX architecture and attention masks. (a) Learnable queries read out the pretrained video backbone’s spatiotemporal representations to encode latent actions. A decoder initialized from the same pretrained backbone reconstructs future video from the latent actions and the initial frame, with auxiliary action supervision when labels are available. (b) Encoder and decoder attention masks control information flow among video, query, and action tokens. In the decoder, video and action tokens read the latent-action queries but do not attend to one another.

visuals.label: Figure 3
visuals.caption: Downstream applications of DreamX. (a) Motion transfer. Source latent actions con- dition the DreamX decoder to generate video from a target initial frame or low-level actions from a target robot state, without paired source–target training data. (b) DreamX policy. A variational bot- tleneck compresses latent actions into compact codes while preserving the token layout. Conditioned on the current observation and instruction, the policy generates these codes alongside low-level ac- tions through a separate DiT action head.

visuals.label: Figure 6
visuals.caption: Qualitative human-to-robot action transfer. Given a human demonstration, DreamX extracts a latent action and decodes it into low-level robot actions without paired human–robot train- ing data. We show diverse transferred behaviors spanning writing, single-arm pushing, and bimanual manipulation. Across substantial embodiment differences, the robot reproduces the motion structure of the human demonstration.
